content: Many individuals engage in stretching exercises either before or after physical activity, often with the intention of minimizing the risk of injury, reducing post-exercise muscle soreness, or improving athletic performance. This review, an update of a Cochrane review first published in 2007, specifically aimed to evaluate the effects of stretching on the development of delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS). To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, and PEDro, up until early 2010. The inclusion criteria required studies to be randomized or quasi-randomized trials that investigated the effects of pre-exercise or post-exercise stretching on DOMS. The stretching interventions had to be performed shortly before or after exercise, and the studies needed to assess muscle soreness as an outcome. The risk of bias in the included studies was evaluated using The Cochrane Collaboration's 'Risk of bias' tool, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The results of the studies were standardized to a 100-point scale, and outcomes were combined using fixed-effect meta-analyses. A total of 12 studies met the inclusion criteria for this review, including two new studies added in this update. One of the new studies was a large field-based trial involving 2,377 participants, of whom 1,220 were assigned to a stretching intervention. The remaining 11 studies were smaller, with sample sizes ranging from 10 to 30 participants in the stretching groups. Ten of these studies were conducted in laboratory settings, while two were field-based. All studies were found to have either a moderate or high risk of bias, and the overall quality of evidence was rated as low to moderate. Despite these limitations, the results across studies were consistent. The pooled data indicated that pre-exercise stretching reduced muscle soreness one day after exercise by an average of 0.5 points on a 100-point scale (mean difference: -0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -11.30 to 10.26; based on three studies). Similarly, post-exercise stretching reduced soreness one day after exercise by an average of 1 point on a 100-point scale (mean difference: -1.04; 95% CI: -6.88 to 4.79; based on four studies). Comparable effects were observed for soreness measured between half a day and three days after exercise. One large study demonstrated that stretching both before and after exercise reduced peak muscle soreness over a one-week period by an average of 4 points on a 100-point scale (mean difference: -3.80; 95% CI: -5.17 to -2.43). While this reduction was statistically significant, the magnitude of the effect was very small and unlikely to be clinically meaningful. In conclusion, the evidence from randomized studies suggests that stretching, whether performed before, after, or both before and after exercise, does not result in clinically significant reductions in delayed-onset muscle soreness in healthy adults.
